units: workmen put up a metal structure in front of the building opposite
the noise of the assembly disturbs the flats on the landing
a sheet stretched over the frontage takes away the tenants' view
the caretaker warns residents that the entry-phone system will be cut off
three households voice their displeasure
a temporary replacement device is adopted
contact between neighbours becomes more frequent
the longest-standing resident finds the situation unheard of
text: Dear neighbour, here is the week as it looked from my window. It began with workmen raising a metal frame against the building opposite, and the clatter of the poles woke every flat on our landing. A green sheet went up over the front of it next, so the courtyard vanished from view. The following morning the caretaker went round the letterboxes, telling us all that the entry-phone would be switched off while the hall was redone. Three households complained, and an agreement followed: a temporary bell, screwed to a plank, would stand in for the handset. By the end of the week the work had already changed our habits. We pass one another on the pavement far more, we stop and chat, and the oldest woman on our stairs says she has known nothing like it since she moved in. Much love.

units: neither the designer nor the residents decide alone how a neighbourhood looks
the shape of a neighbourhood comes out of a long argument between opposing sides
an abandoned plot usually sets off that argument
the emptiness of the place brings out proposals for its use
the proposals bring shared memories back to the surface
what the various sides ask for cannot be reconciled
the local body has to rule between those demands
public conflict usually strengthens attachment to the place
text: Who settles the look of a neighbourhood? Not the architect alone, and not the people who live there either, since the answer comes out of a slow bargaining that sets them against one another as much as it draws them together. What starts that bargaining? An abandoned plot, more often than not: waste ground, thick with nettles, that nobody dares claim. Because the emptiness unsettles people, it draws proposals; and because it draws proposals, it stirs up old memories. And then? One side wants vegetable beds, the other a music room, so the local council is left to rule between wishes that cannot be reconciled. Does the quarrel damage the street? Rarely, say those who have lived through one: by contradicting each other in public they end up acquainted, and their attachment to the place comes out stronger.

units: a maintenance worker sets out a fault to a gathering of occupants
water getting in attacks the connections of the outside panel
every spell of rain cuts the link
an occupant asks whether the whole thing must be replaced
the worker reckons a cover, a new seal and a renewed conduit will do
the woman in charge of the money asks what has to be spent
the sum announced is lower than that of a complete installation
an occupant at the top of the building reports a crackle in her handset
text: The maintenance man set out the fault to the residents' committee. Damp has got into the entry panel, he said, and it is eating the contacts, so the line drops with every shower of rain. One resident asked whether the whole unit would have to go. Not at all, came the answer: a stainless cover, a fresh seal and a length of conduit renewed from the cellar upwards would be enough to dry the circuit out. The treasurer wanted to know what the work would actually cost. He named a modest sum, well under the price of a complete entry-phone, provided the plant room could be reached without clearing it first. A tenant from the top floor mentioned that her handset had been crackling since the autumn. He wrote that down, offered to look at her cable the same afternoon, and closed the panel.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: early communities organised themselves differently according to where they settled
some formed beside a spring, others at a trading crossroads
beside water, authority served to share out a scarce resource
households were counted there and turns of use written down
cheating there brought a loss of standing
at the crossroads, the assembly saw above all to making dealings safe
it standardised the measures and settled disputes
shared memories still differ according to these two origins
present institutions keep the mark of these two models
text: Early communities did not arrange their common life in the same way, and much depended on whether they settled beside a spring or where two trading roads met. In the first case authority went into sharing out what was scarce: households were counted, turns at the water were written down, and anyone who cheated lost standing among the rest. In the second, wealth came from passing traffic, so the assembly worried less about division than about making exchange safe: it fixed the weights, judged disputes and punished sharp practice. Two different sorts of shared memory grew out of that. Where water ruled, what is recalled is shortage and squabbles between neighbours; where trade ruled, the fairs, the ruined merchants and the alliances. Our own institutions still carry the mark of that twofold inheritance.

units: a neighbourhood group rests on supports that can be named
its members first draw up the list of needs and of people available
a place to meet is needed for projects to come to anything
meetings at regular intervals are worth more than occasional enthusiasm
renewing the participants keeps the active core from wearing out
openness about money keeps mistrust away
welcoming newcomers must avoid any unspoken hierarchy
a group deprived of one of these supports survives without drawing anyone new
text: A neighbourhood association rests on supports that are easy enough to pick out. The first is stocktaking: before doing anything, the members list what is needed, and note ages, languages spoken and skills available. The second is a room, because without somewhere to settle, good intentions drift away. The third is regularity, since a meeting held on a fixed date is worth more than a burst of scattered enthusiasm. The fourth is fresh hands: if the same volunteers carry everything, they wear out and the group dies away. The fifth is clarity about money, as the smallest patch of vagueness breeds suspicion. The last is harder to spot: taking newcomers in without saddling them with an unspoken pecking order. An association that neglects one support survives, but it stops drawing anyone in.

units: a musical instrument is taken out through an opening on an upper floor
it is held by a brightly coloured strap
at first the onlookers are very few
a gathering of the curious ends up filling the road
the workman handling the move does not answer the remarks
he rests the load against the frame put up to redo the frontage
a resident fears for her vehicle parked underneath
the arrival on the ground sets off applause
the owner offers a drink to those who watched the scene
she had loathed the object since her marriage
text: You will never guess: a piano came out of a third-floor window on an orange strap. Two or three of us were watching at the start, chins up. Then one passer-by stopped, then another, and in no time the crowd had spread across the road, judging the whole manoeuvre out loud as though it were street theatre. The remover himself said nothing; he hauled on his rope, rested the case against the frame put up to redo the front of the house, let it down a notch and started again. A woman from our stairs was fretting about her car, parked right underneath. When the piano touched the ground the onlookers clapped, which at last got a smile out of him. The best came afterwards: the owner, a very dignified lady, asked the whole pavement in for a drink, to celebrate losing the thing she had hated since her wedding day.

units: clearing a neglected plot calls for organisation beforehand
the landowner's permission decides whether the operation is lawful
without that agreement, nothing covers the damage
an inspection of the ground prevents injuries from buried waste
the jobs must be handed out before the participants arrive
without a share-out arranged in advance, part of the group waits about
protection for the hands and containers in quantity are needed
a heap left behind brings fresh dumping
a shared meal at the end makes participants come back
text: Clearing waste ground calls for a method worked out beforehand, or the volunteers give up after a single outing. Start by getting the landowner to agree: without that, the whole thing is unlawful, and no insurance covers what gets damaged. Then probe the ground, because an old dump can hide broken glass or leaking drums, and a session thrown together ends up at the first-aid post. Hand out the jobs before the group turns up, since if everyone finds out what to do on arrival, half the party is left standing at the gate with nothing to do. Lay in thick gloves and skips enough to take the lot, as one heap left by the roadside pulls in more rubbish. Finish with something to eat together: tiredness sits better when it ends in company, and the volunteers come back for the next outing.

units: an electrical failure leaves a residential area without light
the lifts stopping shuts elderly occupants in at home
those occupants are left without warmth or means of calling
the fault itself is put right quickly
the real obstacle was the lack of information about isolated occupants
a woman working at the library thinks up a cheap solution
an optional register of vulnerable flats is drawn up with the caretaker
two neighbours per floor are named to check the flats when the alarm goes
two later incidents passed off without panic
text: A fault on the grid put the upper part of the neighbourhood into darkness, and the news climbed the stairs, landing by landing. With the lifts at a standstill, elderly residents were held in their flats, without heating and without a charged phone. The trouble lay not in the cut, which was mended quickly enough, but in ignorance: nobody knew who lived alone behind which door. A librarian came up with an answer that was modest and lasting. Together with the caretaker she drew up a voluntary list of the flats where somebody might need help, then gave each floor a pair of neighbours whose job was to knock at the doors the next time. The list sleeps in a sealed envelope. Two alerts have been lived through since, without alarm, and the street claims to feel a good deal less anonymous than before.

units: two stairwells in one and the same block share nothing but their height
one is built on a concrete frame
its broad, straight steps throw sound back
its landings open onto corridors lit by a band of glass
the other, more worn, turns around a stone core
its steps are hollowed by use and its metal rail shifts
its light comes from a glazed opening at the top
the newer stair carries noise from one end of the building to the other
the older stair soaks up sound but holds the damp
the narrowness of the second makes its users meet
text: Two stairwells face each other inside one and the same block of flats, and nothing makes them comparable but their height. The one in the east wing stands on a concrete frame: the steps are straight, broad and loud, and every landing opens onto a corridor lit by a band of glass. The one in the west wing is older and winds round a stone core; the steps are hollowed in the middle by long use, the wrought-iron rail shifts under the hand, and the light drops from a glazed opening right at the top. The first carries sound, so a door slammed at the bottom is heard on the last floor. The second soaks sound up, but it holds the damp, which means repainting the walls rather often. Residents of the older wing see more of each other, since the narrow stair obliges the people who use it to slow down.

units: protecting shared life means naming what makes it fragile
the disappearance of places open to free use is the first threat
all that then remains are places given over to buying
this shift cuts down encounters between people unlike one another
a body that debates without concluding cheapens public speech
the walling-off of the ages separates childhood from old age
alarming stories turn the neighbour into a threat
the writer judges this decline reversible
modest acts such as backing a beginner repair the social bond
text: Standing up for shared life means naming, without any softening, what wears it down. First, the loss of places that cost nothing: as each bench goes, all that is left is space where people buy things, and we stop rubbing along with anyone unlike ourselves. Then the weight of decision, for an assembly that debates at length and never settles anything teaches its members that public speech carries no weight at all. Next comes the sorting of ages, which puts everyone in a separate pen, childhood here, old age elsewhere. To that must be added fear, kept alive by stories that make the neighbour a danger before making him a support. None of this is fated. A society mends itself through ordinary acts: opening a room, backing a beginner, giving up a whole evening to hear out a disagreement.
